1:
Ellicott explains what the chapter is for: the earlier genealogy recognised the heads of families, and here a weightier matter is settled: since Jacob, moved by his love for Rachel, by Joseph's rank and by the spirit of prophecy, bestows on Joseph two tribes; no authority less than his would have sufficed, which is why the grant stands immediately before the blessing of the sons. Calvin frames it differently, that the holy man, knowing himself father of the fathers of the Church, discharged in the prospect of death the prophetic office laid upon him: private persons arrange their affairs by their last wills, and very different was the method of one with whom God had established a covenant. Henry stays with the visit and draws the duties from it, that a sick bed is a proper place both for giving counsel and for receiving instruction, and that it is good to acquaint young people coming into the world with the aged servants of God going out of it.

Clarke uses the second verse to settle a difficulty in the chapter before, holding that Jacob's sitting upon the bed proves a bed and not a staff was meant there; Ellicott adds that the effort was made chiefly because he was about to perform a sacred act under the Divine Spirit. Clarke glosses El Shaddai as the all-sufficient God, the outpourer and dispenser of mercies; Ellicott grounds the act of the chapter on the promise at Bethel, and is the only one detained by the name Luz, which he takes as evidence of how slowly new titles displaced native ones, the names given by Seleucids and Romans in Palestine never having been adopted by the peasantry.

Keil states the legal ground plainly, that the promise of increase and of Canaan as an everlasting possession empowered the patriarch to adopt sons born in Egypt, outside the range of his house. Ellicott works out what follows: Ephraim is reckoned the firstborn and Manasseh the second, the firstborn's legal right being a double share, which is what two tribes amount to; yet the birthright in the spiritual sense was Judah's, Reuben excluded as the penalty of his sin and Simeon and Levi passed over for cruelty. On whether Joseph had later sons Ellicott thinks probably not, while Gill reports Jarchi's conditional reading, that the clause supposes rather than asserts. Calvin will not let the transaction pass without wonder. What is this, he asks, that a decrepit old man assigns to his grandchildren as a royal patrimony a sixth part of the land he entered as a stranger and from which he is now an exile? Who would not say he was dealing in fables, when the proverb is that no one can give what he has not? From which, he concludes, it appears with what firm faith the fathers relied upon the word of the Lord.

Why Rachel is named at all is answered four ways. Ellicott makes it the justification of the act, since Jacob grounds the double portion not on her rank as chief wife but on the untimely death that prevented her bearing more sons. Calvin makes it a spur, that the name of Joseph's mother should move him, since she left her father for a distant land at God's command, and her example ought to induce her sons to bid farewell to Egypt. Clarke makes it pure affection, that Rachel was the wife of Jacob's choice and many waters cannot quench love, and turns it into advice against matches made for convenience or worldly gain, which prove Leah in the place of Rachel to the end of life's pilgrimage. Wesley makes it grief, that strong affections in enjoyment cause long afflictions in the loss. Ellicott adds that the identification with Bethlehem is a note added later, when the place had become famous as the birthplace of David.
8:
The question about the young men is read two ways. Gill and Clarke read it from the blindness: Jacob saw two figures by Joseph but could not distinguish them until they were brought near. Ellicott takes it as a formal turn rather than a failure of sight, the solemn addressing of the discourse to those now to be invested with the patriarchal rank, and adds that they were about eighteen or twenty. Calvin doubts the sequence altogether, holding that Jacob had inquired about the youths before he named them his heirs and that the narrative has placed the question after the event it preceded. Henry draws the blindness out as a lesson, that those who have the honour of age must take its burden with it, and concludes memorably that the eye of faith may be very clear even when the eye of the body is very much clouded. He also notices that the apostle singles out this blessing while passing over the blessing of the rest of the sons, though that too was done in faith.

Joseph's answer draws the most from Calvin. The fruit of the womb is not born by chance but is among the precious gifts of God; the confession finds ready utterance from every tongue, yet few heartily acknowledge that their seed has been given them, and offspring grows continually more degenerate because the ingratitude of the world cannot perceive the effect of God's blessings. Gill supports the sentiment from an unexpected quarter, that it was not a Jewish view only, the names Mattaniah and Nathaniel witnessing to it, but a heathen one as well, the Greeks and Romans forming Theodorus and Apollodorus on the same principle. Wesley finds both men owning God in their comforts, Joseph magnifying the favour by adding that the sons were given him in the place of his banishment; comforts are doubly sweet, he says, when we see them coming from God's hand. Clarke keeps to the tenderness of the words, that Jacob is now amply recompensed for his long grief over a son supposed dead.

Keil supplies the arrangement on which everything after turns. Joseph brought the boys out from between the knees of Israel; then, having prostrated himself, he came up again with Ephraim the younger at his own right hand and Manasseh the elder at his left, so that Ephraim stood at Jacob's right hand and Manasseh at his left. Calvin explains why the removal mattered, that Joseph brought them from his own lap to his father's knees not merely for honour but to present them for a blessing from the prophet of God; and that though the division of the land gave them portions equal with his sons, the imposition of hands looked higher, to their becoming two of the patriarchs of the Church. Ellicott raises a doubt about who performed the act of reverence, since the Samaritan, Syriac and Septuagint treat the verb as a contracted plural, which would make Manasseh and Ephraim the ones who bowed; he judges the pronoun favours the singular.

Clarke turns the same verse into a quarrel with another commentator. Delaney had extolled Joseph's prostration, saying that to see him on his knees to God was to see a mortal at his duty and before Pharaoh a subject before his prince, but that to see him bending to the earth before a poor, old, blind and decrepit father was to behold him with admiration, and to see how such humiliation exalted him. Clarke calls this insufferable, since it says in effect that a young man raised to affluence with scarcely any effort of his own performs a wonder in showing respect to his father, the more gratuitous because the father was poor and blind; the maxim underneath it, he says, is that children who have risen to affluence are not obliged to reverence parents who have been reduced.
13:
Both Keil and Clarke note that the laying on of hands appears here for the first time in Scripture and list the same later uses. Keil defines it as a symbolical sign by which the one acting transferred to another a spiritual good, a supersensual power or gift. Clarke instead draws a pattern from the reversal, that God has from the beginning preferred the younger to the elder, Abel before Cain, Isaac before Ishmael, Jacob before Esau, Ephraim before Manasseh, Moses before Aaron and David before his brethren, and resolves the whole of it into the wise and secret counsel of God. Ellicott raises a question about the words describing the act: the Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate render them placing his hands crosswise, while Onkelos supports the received rendering, guiding his hands wittingly; there is some philological support for the three chief versions, he allows, though it must rest mainly on their own authority, which is however very great. Calvin keeps to the received sense and presses the deliberateness, that a man too dim-sighted to distinguish the boys nevertheless crossed his hands on purpose, not moving them from one head to the other by feeling, from which he gathers that the Holy Spirit directed the act. Gill supplies the mechanics, that Joseph had placed each boy to receive the hand he intended, and that Jacob stretched his right hand not forward but across.

Clarke notes the order, that the father is blessed first and the sons afterwards, and takes it for proof of Jacob's superiority, since the less is always blessed of the greater. Gill reads the blessing of Joseph as a blessing in his sons, reckoned for him and made heads of tribes in his room. The clause about God feeding him draws the warmest comment. Clarke has Jacob standing on the verge of eternity with his faith strong, seeing his life as a series of mercies and perceiving that he owes every morsel of food to mere kindness; Wesley turns it forward, that our bodies have called for daily food and we have never wanted food convenient, and that he who has fed us all our life long will not fail us at last. Calvin finds a rule for the ministry in the fact that Jacob, knowing a dispensation of grace was committed to him, still arrogates nothing but resorts to prayer: pastors entrusted with the dispensation of spiritual gifts are nothing compared with God, so let them keep their own place lest they obscure his name, since mortal man cannot without sacrilege desire to seem anything separate from God.

The Angel who redeemed him is identified with Christ by all four who touch it, but by four different arguments. Gill argues from the works predicated: the deliverance meant is not only preservation from Esau and Laban but redemption from the guilt and punishment of sin and from everlasting wrath, and none but a divine Person could do these, nor would Jacob have asked them of a creature. Clarke argues from the word, that the Hebrew calls him the Messenger and the Goel, a term the law applies to the man whose right it is, as nearest of kin, to redeem a forfeited inheritance; and only he who took part of our flesh and blood can be that kinsman. Calvin argues from the worship, that Jacob so joins the Angel to God as to make him his equal, asking the same things of him as of God, which would be absurd of a created angel; it must therefore be Christ, who does not bear the title of Angel in vain because he had become the perpetual Mediator. Wesley simply asserts it, that Christ the angel of the covenant redeems us from all evil, and adds that it becomes the servants of God, when they are old and dying, to witness that they have found him gracious.
17:
Joseph's objection is explained two ways. Clarke makes it natural affection working on a universal convention, that the right hand was reckoned the nobler and the instrument of the highest dignities; his summary is that Joseph spoke as moved by natural affection and Jacob acted as influenced by the Holy Spirit. Calvin will not have the objection put down to partiality: Joseph thought the error arose from dimness of vision, but his displeasure arose from faith and from holy reverence for the prophetic office, since he would easily have borne the same thing had it been his father's own doing rather than a prophet's. Gill supplies the custom being crossed, that the blessing was thought to belong to the firstborn, though it had not always gone so, as Jacob's own case showed.

How the prophecy was fulfilled is where the witnesses part company, neither noticing the other. Ellicott reports that at the final numbering on the plains of Moab Manasseh had fifty-two thousand seven hundred and Ephraim only thirty-two thousand five hundred, so that on the figures the greatness went the wrong way; his explanation is that the division of Manasseh made it politically insignificant while Ephraim obtained a commanding position, that Joshua being an Ephraimite the tribe held the foremost rank ever after, and that the ark was placed in one of its towns. He adds a comparison of his own, that Joshua after the conquest must have held a position like General Washington's after American independence. Wesley draws the opposite picture from a different census, that at the mustering in the wilderness Ephraim was the more numerous and had the standard of that squadron; he agrees only on the division of Manasseh across the Jordan as the cause of its weakness. Keil states the refusal without comment.

Both Calvin and Wesley turn the reversal into a doctrine of divine freedom. Calvin holds that Jacob does not dispute which youth is worthier but pronounces what God had decreed, that our dignity is hidden in the counsel of God alone until his vocation makes plain what he wills, and that they are altogether insane who hew out dry and perforated cisterns in seeking causes of divine adoption, since the primary source of election is God's free good pleasure. Wesley says that God gives more to some than to others, and often most to those least likely, choosing the weak things of the world and raising the poor out of the dust, so that grace does not observe the order of nature nor does God prefer those we think fittest, but as it pleases him.

Clarke and Ellicott both record that the blessing became a formula, Ellicott that the Israelites still use Jacob's words over their children, Clarke that Jewish women say to their daughters at marriage, God make thee as Sarah and Rebekah. On the announcement of death Gill notes that Jacob speaks of it not with dread but with pleasure, and Clarke builds an argument on that composure: could men act as the patriarchs did in their last moments who had no hope of eternal life and no belief in the immortality of the soul, and suppose themselves creatures of a day, on whom God had wasted so much care only that they should end like the beasts that perish? Calvin takes the same words as instruction rather than evidence, that Jacob mentions his death to teach that the truth of God does not depend on the life of men, his own life passing away while the promise, which has no limit, will flourish when he is dead; no vision had appeared to his sons, so he took timely precaution that their faith should not be shaken by his death. Wesley makes it pastoral, that the assurance was preserved so they might neither love Egypt when it favoured them nor fear it when it frowned.
22:
The word rendered portion is in Hebrew one Shechem, and what it means is the first question. Gill reports that some take it not as a common noun but as the name of the city, the Targum of Jonathan and Jarchi so interpreting it, and holds that the city is referred to though not directly meant, since the parcel lay near it and the city with all the country about it fell to Ephraim. Calvin has no doubt a definite territory is meant and thinks the question closed by the evangelist, who says of the field adjoining Sychar that it was what Jacob gave to Joseph; he rejects the alternative some proposed, that Jacob merely calls Joseph a double heir in his two sons. Ellicott alone argues both sides. For the town he sets the facts that it did belong to Jacob, that Joseph's embalmed body was laid there in ground bought for a hundred kesitas, and that a parcel at Sychar is identified in the gospel with the ground given him. Against it he sets the objection that one Shechem is an unnatural way of describing a town, and the lexical point, on Abul-walid's authority, that the word also means the shoulder and was given to any elevated strip of ground. His resolution is a play upon words, the plot of hill-ground being called a Shechem rather than by the ordinary term for a ridge, in order to show that the town was the portion really signified.

The claim to have taken it with sword and bow is harder, since the same ground is elsewhere said to have been bought. Four answers are offered and one refusal. Wesley supplies a history: Jacob purchased the land first, was afterwards dispossessed by the Amorites, and retook it by the sword, recovering his right by violence when he could not recover it otherwise. Calvin argues from the price, that only a place to pitch his tents was bought, as anyone may calculate from the hundred pieces of silver, so that what he now gives Joseph takes in the much larger field which had been the common land of the city. Ellicott addresses the other half of the phrase, that Shechem was strictly a Hivite town, but that since they were a feeble tribe the name Amorite may have been used to give the exploit greater glory. Gill denies the premises: the place was taken not from the Amorite but from the Hivite, and not by sword and bow at all. Both refuse the obvious candidate, the sack of the city by Simeon and Levi, Gill because Jacob would never make his own act a deed he so abhorred and still abhorred in the chapter following, Ellicott because a man who condemns that exploit so strongly can scarcely be claiming it.

Clarke declines to answer at all. How it could be said that Jacob took this from the Amorite with his sword and his bow, he writes, we cannot tell; many attempts have been made to explain the verse and all have hitherto been fruitless; the words were no doubt well understood by Joseph and probably alluded to some transaction not now on record; and it is much safer to confess our ignorance than to hazard conjecture after conjecture. Calvin, who does conjecture, still rules one out, calling the interpretation that sword and bow stand figuratively for prayer and supplication still more improbable than the rest. Wesley closes on the ground itself, that the parcel was given to Ephraim as their right and the lot was never cast upon it, that Joseph's bones were buried in it, which he suspects Jacob had as much in view as anything, and that while it may sometimes be just and prudent to give some children portions above the rest, a grave is what we can most count upon as our own in this earth.
